newsitem.title: USA: US envoy sees China policy unaffected by scandal.
newsitem.headline: US envoy sees China policy unaffected by scandal.

text.p: U.S. ambassador to China James Sasser said on Thursday a fund-raising scandal allegedly involving Chinese embassy officials was unlikely to derail Washington's policies towards Beijing.

"The administration is in the process of formulating, or has formulated the policies towards China," Sasser said at a luncheon address organised by the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations. "I don't think they are going to be deterred by stories of campaign contributions."

The Justice Department is investigating reports that Chinese embassy officials in Washington sought to secretly steer foreign donations towards President Bill Clinton's 1996 re-election campaign. The Chinese embassy has denied the allegation.

Sasser, who was sworn in as U.S. ambassador to China in January 1996 after three terms as senator from Tennessee, said he did not know much about the campaign contributions scandal and the opinions he expressed were his personal views.

He warned that the widening U.S. trade deficit with China would continue to be an irritant in bilateral ties. By U.S. count, the trade deficit reached $40 billion, although the Chinese challenged the statistics.
But there are bright spots on the trade front.

The recently concluded textile agreement, for the first time, provided meaningful access for U.S. producers into the Chinese market and improved procedures dealing with illegal trans-shipment, Sasser said.
He called human rights "the most taxing issue," and said the United States would seek to impress on China that political freedom was key to the country's long-term properity and stability.
He said he was encouraged by signs of expanding personal liberty, legal rights and incipient village democracy in China.
Sasser expected Vice President Al Gore to visit China later this month and Chinese President Jiang Zemin to come to the United States this fall.
